title: Action Research for Teachers

pts: Action research is a structured cycle of planning, acting, observing and reflecting, applied to a teacher's own genuine classroom question.
This formalises and extends Unit 9's reflective practice into a more rigorous, evidence-based investigative process.
It's designed to be conducted by practitioners themselves, not only by outside researchers studying a classroom from a distance.
points.who: Kurt Lewin's action research model; applied to education by Kemmis & McTaggart

v: A blank A4 sheet; a recent classroom problem

items: Draw four boxes in a circle: Plan, Act, Observe, Reflect.
Think of one recent change you made in class, however small.
Fill each box for that change: what you planned, what you did, what you noticed, what you concluded.
Mark any box that was based on impression rather than evidence.
Discuss with a partner how the cycle would change if you repeated it with evidence.
In a DIET pre-service session, trainees map a lesson from their practice teaching.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One teacher’s first attempt (written for this book):

lines: Plan: use pair work before whole-class answers.
Act: did it for a week in Class 8.
Observe: ‘seemed better’.
Reflect: ‘pair work works’.

blocks.x: The Observe box shows the gap. ‘Seemed better’ is an impression. Action research asks: better in what way, by how much, and how do you know?

pts: A good action research question comes from a genuine, specific classroom puzzle — not an imposed or overly broad theoretical question.
'Does delayed correction improve accuracy more than immediate correction in my speaking classes?' is more workable than 'is task-based learning effective?'
Specificity and genuine personal investment in the question sustain the multi-cycle process this method requires.

v: A list of classroom puzzles; a partner

items: Write down three things that puzzle or bother you about your English classes.
Choose the one you care about most.
Narrow it: which learners, which skill, which kind of lesson?
Rewrite it as a question about something you can change and observe.
Check it with a partner against three tests: Is it specific? Is it within my control? Can I collect evidence on it in four to six weeks?
Exploratory start: phrase a ‘why’ question first (Allwright and Hanks 2009), then an action question once you understand the puzzle.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Too broad: Is task-based learning effective?
Better: Do my Class 9 learners speak more in English during group tasks?
Workable: Does giving two minutes of planning time before a group speaking task increase the number of English turns in my Class 9B groups?
A: My puzzle is that the back benches never speak.
B: Is that about seating, confidence or the task?
A: I don’t know yet. Maybe my first question should be ‘why’.

body: Purpose: to show how a broad worry becomes a researchable question. Content: a funnel with a broad worry at the top, narrower versions in the middle and a precise question at the bottom. Style: simple infographic. Board version: a triangle with three lines of text.

items: Google Docs (free) for drafting and sharing questions with a critical friend.

body: If a question could be answered by reading a book, it is probably not an action research question. Good questions are about your learners, your lessons and your context.

pts: Design a specific, clearly describable change to try, informed by existing methodology and theory from earlier posters in this series.
The intervention should be genuinely implementable within real classroom constraints, not a idealised version impossible to sustain.
Document the plan clearly enough that another teacher could understand exactly what was actually done.

v: The research question; a relevant unit of this book

items: Find a principle in earlier units that relates to the question (for example, planning time in Unit 29).
Describe the change in three to five sentences: what, when, with whom, for how long.
Check it is sustainable: could you do it every lesson for four weeks with 50 learners?
Decide what will stay the same so that the change can be seen clearly.
Ask a colleague to read the card and explain back what you will do.
Plan a simple comparison: the same task with and without the change, in two lessons.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: An intervention card (written for this book):

lines: Question: Does two minutes of silent planning before group speaking increase English turns in Class 9B?
Change: Before each group task, learners get two minutes to note ideas and key words, in any language, on a slip.
Duration: three lessons a week for four weeks.
Kept the same: group size (four), task type (opinion exchange), time (eight minutes).

blocks.x: Allowing notes in any language is a deliberate choice: the teacher can later check whether home-language planning supports English output.

body: Purpose: to model a clear, describable change. Content: an index card with headings Question, Change, Duration, Kept the same, pinned to a corkboard beside a class timetable. Style: realistic, handwritten look. Board version: four headings in a box.

pts: Combine multiple data sources — student work samples, brief surveys, error logs (Unit 8), recorded observations — rather than relying on general impression alone.
Triangulating multiple evidence sources strengthens confidence in the findings beyond what any single source could support alone.
This connects to Unit 49's systematic error analysis as one concrete evidence-gathering method available within this cycle.

v: Tally sheets; a short learner survey; learner work samples

items: Choose at least three evidence sources: for example, a tally of English turns, a two-question learner survey and a sample of written notes.
Prepare simple instruments before the first lesson.
Collect a baseline in one or two lessons before the change.
Collect the same evidence during the intervention.
Keep a short research diary after each lesson.
Ask a colleague to observe one group with the tally sheet (see Unit 68).
Use an error log (Unit 8) or an error analysis (Unit 49) as one source.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: When three sources point the same way, confidence grows. When they disagree, the disagreement is itself a finding. This combination of sources is called triangulation (Burns 2010).

body: Purpose: to show three sources converging on one finding. Content: a triangle with a tally sheet, a survey and a notebook at its corners, with lines meeting at a central point labelled ‘finding’. Style: clean diagram. Board version: a triangle with three labels.

pts: Look for patterns across the collected evidence, comparing against what was expected or hoped for from the intervention.
Genuine reflection here means being honest about ambiguous, mixed, or even negative results, not just confirming the expected outcome.
This is where the discipline of action research most distinguishes itself from casual, confirmation-biased reflection.

items: Put baseline and intervention evidence side by side.
Summarize each source in one sentence.
Note where results match expectations, where they do not, and where they are unclear.
Ask your critical friend to suggest at least one other explanation for the results.
Write a cautious conclusion that the evidence supports.
In a DIET research group, participants swap data sets and interpret each other’s evidence first.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Tally: English turns rose from an average of 11 to 17 per group.
Survey: 31 of 46 learners said planning helped; 9 said ‘a little’; 6 said ‘no’.
Notes: most slips were in Kannada with English key words.
Diary: two groups used the time to chat.

blocks.x: Cautious conclusion: Planning time seems to have increased English turns in most groups, and home-language notes did not reduce English output. Two groups did not use the time well; the task instructions may need changing.

lines: A: Could the rise be because the topics were easier that week?
B: Possibly. I’ll keep the topics at the same level next cycle.

body: Researchers call the tendency to notice evidence that supports what we already believe confirmation bias. A critical friend who asks ‘What else could explain this?’ is one of the simplest protections against it.

pts: Action research is typically cyclical — findings from one cycle inform a refined intervention for the next, rather than a single final verdict.
This mirrors Unit 9's reflective-practice cycle, now formalised with more deliberate structure and evidence collection across multiple iterations.
A single cycle can still yield useful insight, but the method's real strength emerges across sustained iteration.

items: List what cycle one showed, what it left unclear and what went wrong.
Decide on one refinement to the intervention.
Decide on one refinement to the evidence collection.
Write a new intervention card.
Set a date to review both cycles together.
Hand the refined cycle to a colleague who teaches a parallel class and compare results.

lines: Refinement: planning slips now have three headings (‘My idea’, ‘My reason’, ‘Useful English words’) to keep planning on task.
Evidence change: tally all ten groups once a week, not one group every lesson.
Keep: two minutes, any language allowed on the slip.

blocks.x: The first cycle rarely gives a final answer. It gives a better second question, which is how the spiral rises (Kemmis and McTaggart 1988).

pts: Sharing action research findings with colleagues, even informally, extends its value beyond a single teacher's individual practice.
This connects directly to Unit 68's mentoring and peer observation, and to professional development communities more broadly.
Even modest, small-scale findings can meaningfully inform colleagues facing similar classroom questions.

Chart paper; findings from at least one cycle

items: Divide the chart paper into five sections: Question, What I changed, Evidence, What I found, What next.
Write no more than three lines in each section.
Add one chart or learner quotation.
Present it in a five-minute slot at a staff meeting, cluster meeting or teacher learning community.
Invite two questions and one suggestion from colleagues.
Share the poster in a teachers’ WhatsApp group or at a teacher association conference.

pts: Systematic evidence from action research can inform genuine scheme-of-work (Unit 14) or institutional policy changes, beyond just an individual teacher's own practice.
This gives teacher-conducted research a real, structured pathway from individual curiosity into wider practical influence.
This connects the practitioner directly to the kind of evidence-based decision-making Tier IV explores at greater theoretical depth.

Findings from one or more teachers; the current scheme of work

items: Collect two or three action research findings on related questions from colleagues.
Identify a decision they bear on, such as the use of planning time in the scheme of work (Unit 14).
Draft a short proposal: the finding, the evidence, the proposed change, and how its effect will be checked.
Present it to the head of department, principal or DIET research committee.
If adopted, plan a school-wide cycle to monitor the change.

dek: Unit 67 of 100: a structured method for systematically investigating your own classroom questions — turning Unit 9's reflective practice into genuine, disciplined inquiry.

aims.x: Every teacher has classroom questions: why a group stays silent, whether a new correction technique works, why homework is copied. Reflection helps us notice such questions. Action research helps us answer them with evidence. This unit sets out a practical, small-scale version of the action research cycle that a busy teacher in a government or private school can manage alongside a full timetable.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: describe the plan–act–observe–reflect cycle and its origins;
turn a classroom puzzle into a focused, answerable question;
design an intervention that is clear, realistic and describable;
collect evidence from at least three sources and triangulate it;
analyse mixed or negative results honestly;
plan a second cycle from the findings of the first;
share findings with colleagues in a short, usable format;
use classroom evidence to argue for changes in a scheme of work or school policy.

why: Why this matters. Reflection alone can drift into impression and anecdote. Action research adds enough structure to actually know whether a change you made worked.

background.x: The term action research is usually traced to the social psychologist Kurt Lewin (1946), who described a spiral of planning, action and fact-finding about the results of action. In education, Lawrence Stenhouse (1975) argued that teachers should be researchers of their own classrooms rather than only consumers of research done by others. Stephen Kemmis and Robin McTaggart (1988) developed the widely used four-moment cycle of plan, act, observe, reflect, repeated as a spiral. In English language teaching, Michael Wallace (1998) and Anne Burns (2010) wrote practical guides that show how language teachers can carry out such cycles within ordinary teaching.

Action research differs from general reflection (Unit 9, and Unit 72 at greater depth) in its discipline. The teacher states a question, makes a deliberate change, collects evidence systematically and draws conclusions that the evidence can support. It differs from academic research in its purpose: its first aim is to improve practice in one setting, not to produce findings that generalize to all classrooms. A related tradition, exploratory practice, suggests that teachers can begin by understanding a puzzle before trying to solve it (Allwright and Hanks 2009), and exploratory action research combines the two (Smith and Rebolledo 2018).

India has a lively tradition of teacher research. DIETs have long encouraged action research by teacher educators and teachers, and teacher associations such as AINET have supported networks of teacher researchers [VERIFY current AINET programmes]. NEP 2020 describes teachers as professionals who should have autonomy and continuous professional development, and NCF 2023 encourages teachers to reflect on and adapt their practice (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Action research gives these aims a concrete method. It also invites questions about home languages: for example, whether allowing brief Kannada or Telugu discussion before an English task improves the English that follows. A school’s own evidence on such a question is often more persuasive to colleagues than any external claim.

items: Research question. A focused question that passes the three tests of specificity, control and feasibility.
Intervention card. A clearly described, sustainable change with the constants noted.
Evidence file. At least three types of evidence, with baseline and intervention data.
Research poster. A one-page summary presented to colleagues, with a cautious conclusion and a next step.
Which classroom puzzle have you been carrying for longest? Why have you not investigated it?
What counts as evidence in your classroom, and what do you usually rely on instead?
How do you respond when results do not match what you hoped for?
Who could be your critical friend?
How could your learners take part in the research, not only be its subjects?
What question about home-language use would you most like evidence on?

terms.def: Small-scale, systematic enquiry by teachers into a problem in their own classroom, moving through cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting; for example, testing whether a new seating plan increases pair talk.
Evidence collected before a change is introduced, against which later results can be compared; in action research, a teacher might record pair-talk time in two lessons before trying a new technique.
The tendency to notice and value evidence that supports what we already believe; in action research, a critical friend helps guard against it.
A trusted colleague who asks challenging questions and offers honest feedback on a teacher’s work or research, including other possible explanations for results.

A form of practitioner research in which teachers and learners work together to understand puzzles in their classroom life, using normal teaching activities as the means of investigation (Allwright and Hanks 2009).
In action research, the planned change a teacher makes in order to address a classroom question, described clearly enough that its effects can be observed and evaluated.

The repeated sequence of steps in action research: identifying a problem, planning an intervention, acting, observing and collecting evidence, and reflecting, which then leads to a revised plan and a new cycle.

A dated record kept by a teacher-researcher during an enquiry, noting observations, decisions, learner responses and developing interpretations. It is a source of evidence in its own right and supports honest reflection on the research process.

A clear, focused question that a piece of research sets out to answer, such as ‘Does five minutes of daily pair talk increase how much my Class 7 learners speak in English?’ A good one is specific and answerable with available evidence.

Using several sources, methods or perspectives to check findings, for example combining learner interviews, employer views and document analysis in needs analysis, or observation and learner work in action research.
